title: Subsidiary Books
outcomes: Explain why the journal is split into subsidiary books and how this helps division of work and control.
Record credit purchases, credit sales and returns in the purchases, sales and returns books at net (after trade discount) values.
Post the subsidiary books: monthly totals to the nominal accounts and individual amounts to the parties.
Identify transactions that belong in the journal proper, and add GST columns to subsidiary books.

meta.exam_tip: The most common trap: putting a credit purchase of an asset, or a cash purchase, into the purchases book. Only credit purchases of goods go there.

concepts.title: Why split the journal?
body: A busy business has hundreds of similar transactions. Recording them all in one journal is slow and hard to post. So similar transactions are grouped into separate "subsidiary" (special) books.

Benefits: work can be divided among staff; posting is faster because only totals go to the nominal account; errors are easier to locate; and each book gives instant information (total credit sales this month, for example).
concepts.analogy: A hospital has separate counters for registration, pharmacy and billing instead of one long queue — faster, and everyone knows where to look.
concepts.work: Modern software keeps "registers" — purchase register, sales register, debit note register. These are subsidiary books under another name, and auditors download them first.

concepts.title: Purchases book
body: Records only credit purchases of goods (goods bought for resale or for production). Entries are made from supplier invoices, at the net amount after trade discount.
Posting: each supplier's account is credited with its invoice amount; the monthly total is debited to Purchases Account.
Not recorded here: cash purchases (cash book) and purchases of assets on credit (journal proper).
concepts.analogy: A list of everything you bought on "khata" (credit) for your shop shelves.
concepts.work: Before an invoice is entered, accounts teams match it with the purchase order and the goods received note — the "three-way match" that prevents paying for goods never received.

concepts.title: Sales book
body: Records only credit sales of goods, from copies of the invoices issued, at net value after trade discount.
Posting: each customer's account is debited; the monthly total is credited to Sales Account. Cash sales go to the cash book; credit sale of an old asset goes to the journal proper.
concepts.analogy: The mirror image of the purchases book — what customers took on credit.
concepts.work: At the year end auditors check "cut-off": invoices dated 31 March must relate to goods actually dispatched by 31 March, otherwise sales are overstated.

concepts.title: Returns books, debit notes and credit notes
body: Purchase Returns (Returns Outward) Book: goods returned to suppliers. The buyer sends a debit note — "we are debiting your account". Posting: supplier debited; total credited to Purchase Returns Account.

Sales Returns (Returns Inward) Book: goods returned by customers. The seller issues a credit note — "we are crediting your account". Posting: customer credited; total debited to Sales Returns Account.
Returns are valued at the same net price at which the goods were bought or sold.
concepts.analogy: A debit note says "I am reducing what I owe you"; a credit note says "I am reducing what you owe me".
concepts.work: Unmatched debit notes are a frequent cause of differences in supplier balance confirmations — the supplier simply has not recorded the return yet.

concepts.title: Journal proper
body: Entries that do not fit any subsidiary book still go to the journal: opening and closing entries, adjustment entries (outstanding, prepaid, depreciation), rectification entries, transfer entries, and credit purchase or sale of assets.
Also: goods withdrawn by the owner, goods lost by fire or theft, bad debts written off and interest on capital or drawings.
concepts.analogy: The "miscellaneous" drawer — small, but you cannot run the house without it.
concepts.work: Auditors look closely at journal entries passed at the year end, because unusual adjustments here can change profit significantly.

concepts.title: GST columns in subsidiary books
body: A GST-registered business adds columns for the taxable value and each tax: CGST and SGST (supply within the State) or IGST (supply to another State).
Posting: taxable value total to Sales (or Purchases); tax column totals to the Output (or Input) tax accounts; the full invoice value to each party.

jobs.title: Entering supplier invoices the right way
jobs.role: Accounts payable executive in a manufacturing company
jobs.situation: A stack of 40 supplier invoices arrives. Two have no purchase order, one bills 500 units though the stores received 480, and one is for a new air conditioner for the office.
steps: Match each invoice with its purchase order and goods received note (three-way match).
Hold the invoices without a purchase order and ask the buyer to confirm.
For the short supply, enter the full invoice and raise a debit note for 20 units — or ask the supplier for a revised invoice.
The air conditioner is an asset: it goes through the journal (or asset register), not the purchases register.
jobs.takeaway: Subsidiary book rules are internal controls in disguise — they stop wrong or fake purchases from reaching the accounts.
jobs.think: Why should the person who enters invoices not be the person who approves payments?
jobs.answer: Separating duties means one person alone cannot both create a liability and pay it — it reduces the chance of fraud or error going unnoticed.

jobs.title: Sales cut-off test at the year end
jobs.situation: Your senior asks you to test sales cut-off for a distributor. You select invoices dated 28 March to 4 April.
steps: For each invoice, check the dispatch document (delivery challan, transport receipt) date.
Invoices dated before 31 March but goods sent in April overstate this year's sales.
Also check credit notes issued in April for goods returned that were sold in March.
jobs.takeaway: The sales book records invoices — the auditor checks that each invoice really belongs to the year.
jobs.think: An invoice for ₹2,00,000 is dated 31 March but the goods left on 2 April. What is the effect on this year's accounts?
jobs.answer: Sales and debtors are overstated by ₹2,00,000 (and closing stock understated by its cost), so profit is overstated by the margin on that sale.

mcqs.q: Credit purchase of furniture for office use is recorded in the:
options: Journal proper
Purchases book
Cash book
Purchase returns book
mcqs.explain: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods meant for resale. Office furniture is an asset, not stock-in-trade, so its credit purchase does not fit any special subsidiary book and is recorded in the journal proper: Furniture A/c Dr. To Supplier A/c. The tempting option, the purchases book, would wrongly inflate purchases and cost of goods sold. In practice: auditors check that capital items are not hidden in purchases, since that would understate profit and fixed assets.

mcqs.q: The total of the sales book is posted to:
options: The credit side of Sales Account
The debit side of Sales Account
The credit side of each customer's account
The debit side of Cash Account
mcqs.explain: Each credit sale in the sales book is posted to the debit of the individual customer's account. At the end of the period, the total of the sales book is posted to the credit side of Sales Account, completing the double entry. The tempting option, crediting each customer, reverses the customer posting — customers who buy on credit owe money, so they are debited. In practice: accounting software posts each invoice to the customer ledger and the monthly total to Sales automatically.

mcqs.q: When goods are returned to a supplier, the buyer sends a:
options: Debit note
Credit note
Invoice
Receipt
mcqs.explain: When the buyer returns goods to a supplier, the buyer reduces the amount owed by debiting the supplier's account, and informs the supplier through a debit note. The tempting option, a credit note, is the document the supplier (seller) issues on accepting the return, because the seller credits the buyer's account. In practice: under GST, the supplier issues a credit note to reduce output tax, while the buyer's debit note is the buyer's own record.
mcqs.topic: Purchase Returns or Returns Outward Book

mcqs.q: Goods with a list price of ₹24,000 are sold on credit at 15% trade discount. The amount entered in the sales book is:
mcqs.explain: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice before recording and never appears in the books: ₹24,000 × 85% = ₹20,400 is entered in the sales book. The tempting ₹24,000 records the list price, but the customer never owes that amount. ₹3,600 is the trade discount itself. In practice: wholesalers offer trade discounts to retailers on the printed list price, and GST is charged on the discounted value shown on the invoice.

mcqs.q: Which transaction is recorded in the purchases book of a furniture dealer?
options: Furniture bought on credit for resale
Furniture bought for cash for resale
A computer bought on credit for the office
Furniture returned to the supplier
mcqs.explain: The purchases book records credit purchases of goods in which the business deals. For a furniture dealer, furniture is stock-in-trade, so furniture bought on credit for resale goes in the purchases book. The tempting option, furniture bought for cash for resale, is a purchase of goods but is recorded in the cash book, not the purchases book. The computer for office use is an asset, recorded in the journal proper. In practice: dealers' purchase registers list only supplier credit invoices.

mcqs.q: The total of the sales returns book is posted to:
options: The debit side of Sales Returns Account
The credit side of Sales Returns Account
The debit side of Sales Account
The credit side of Purchases Account
mcqs.explain: Sales returns reduce sales. Each return is credited to the customer's account (they owe less), and the period total of the sales returns book is posted to the debit side of Sales Returns Account. The tempting option, the credit side, would increase the returns account's opposite balance and leave the double entry one-sided. In practice: the sales returns total is deducted from sales in the trading account to show net sales.
mcqs.topic: Sales Returns Book or Returns Inward Book

mcqs.q: An intra-State credit sale of ₹50,000 attracts CGST and SGST of 6% each. The customer is debited with:
mcqs.explain: For an intra-State supply, CGST and SGST are charged: CGST 6% of ₹50,000 = ₹3,000 and SGST 6% = ₹3,000. The customer is debited with the full invoice value: ₹50,000 + ₹6,000 = ₹56,000. The tempting ₹53,000 counts only one of the two taxes. In practice: the sales book of a GST-registered business has separate columns for taxable value, CGST, SGST and IGST, and the customer column shows the invoice total.

mcqs.q: An entry for depreciation on machinery is made in the:
options: Journal proper
Purchases book
Sales book
Cash book
mcqs.explain: Depreciation is an adjustment entry that involves no cash, no purchase and no sale of goods, so it fits no special subsidiary book and is recorded in the journal proper: Depreciation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c. The tempting option, the cash book, records only cash and bank transactions, and depreciation involves no payment. In practice: year-end adjustments — depreciation, outstanding and prepaid expenses, provisions — are all passed as journal vouchers in Tally.

questions.q: What is the journal proper? Give four kinds of entries that are recorded in it, with one example each.

model.text: The journal proper is the book in which transactions that cannot be recorded in any subsidiary book (cash book, purchases, sales, returns books) are entered.

items: Opening entry — bringing forward last year's asset and liability balances.
Adjustment entries — outstanding salary, prepaid insurance, depreciation.
Rectification entries — correcting a sale wrongly posted to another customer.
Credit purchase or sale of assets — machinery bought on credit.
Transfer and closing entries — transferring expenses to the Profit and Loss Account.

summary: Subsidiary books group similar transactions: purchases, sales, purchase returns, sales returns (plus the cash book).
Purchases and sales books record only credit transactions in goods, at net value after trade discount.
Parties are posted individually; the period total goes to the nominal account.
Returns: debit note (to supplier), credit note (to customer), valued at net price.
Everything else goes to the journal proper.

Sales book → total credited to Sales A/c.

traps: Don't record assets or cash transactions in the purchases or sales book.
Don't value returns at list price.
Don't show trade discount as a separate posting.

viva.q: Why does a business keep subsidiary books instead of only one journal?
viva.model: Subsidiary books group similar transactions together. This allows division of work among staff, saves time because only the periodic totals are posted to the nominal accounts, makes errors easier to locate, and gives quick information such as the total credit sales of the month.

cases.title: Raj Electricals — sales book with GST
cases.case: Raj Electricals of Jaipur (Rajasthan) is registered under GST. In October 2026 it sells goods on credit to Amit of Kota (Rajasthan) for ₹50,000 plus CGST 9% and SGST 9%, and to Bhavna of Indore (Madhya Pradesh) for ₹30,000 plus IGST 18%. Later in the month Amit returns goods with a taxable value of ₹5,000 (with the related tax).

mcqs.q: With what amount is Amit's account debited for the sale?
mcqs.explain: Amit is in Rajasthan, the same State as Raj, so CGST and SGST apply: CGST 9% = ₹4,500 and SGST 9% = ₹4,500. Amit is debited with the full invoice value: ₹50,000 + ₹4,500 + ₹4,500 = ₹59,000. The tempting ₹54,500 adds only one tax. In practice: the customer owes the whole invoice including tax, and the seller later pays the tax collected to the government.

mcqs.q: How much IGST is charged to Bhavna?
mcqs.explain: Bhavna is in Madhya Pradesh, so the supply is inter-State and IGST is charged instead of CGST and SGST: ₹30,000 × 18% = ₹5,400. The tempting ₹2,700 is 9%, wrongly splitting the rate as if it were an intra-State supply. IGST is a single tax at the combined rate. In practice: the place of supply decides whether an invoice carries IGST or CGST plus SGST, and getting it wrong means paying the correct tax again.

mcqs.q: Which total from the sales book is credited to Sales Account?
mcqs.explain: Sales Account is credited only with the taxable value; GST collected is a liability to the government and goes to the Output CGST, SGST and IGST accounts. Total taxable sales = ₹50,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹80,000. The tempting ₹94,400 includes the tax collected, which would overstate sales by ₹14,400 (₹9,000 + ₹5,400). In practice: GST returns report taxable value and tax separately, and the books must match them.

mcqs.q: Which document and book record Amit's return?
options: Credit note issued by Raj; Sales Returns Book
Debit note issued by Raj; Purchases Returns Book
Credit note issued by Amit; Sales Book
Debit note issued by Raj; Sales Returns Book
mcqs.explain: When a customer returns goods, the seller credits the customer's account and informs the customer through a credit note. Raj records the return in its Sales Returns (Returns Inward) Book. The tempting option, a debit note issued by Raj, is wrong because a debit note is sent by the party returning goods, here Amit. In practice: under GST, the supplier's credit note reduces its output tax liability and must be reported in its returns.
mcqs.topic: Sales Returns Book or Returns Inward Book

mcqs.q: What is the net Output CGST for October after the return?
mcqs.explain: Output CGST on Amit's sale was 9% of ₹50,000 = ₹4,500. The return of ₹5,000 reduces it by 9% of ₹5,000 = ₹450, so net output CGST = ₹4,050. The IGST sale to Bhavna carries no CGST. The tempting ₹4,500 ignores the credit note's tax reversal. In practice: GST-registered businesses adjust output tax for credit notes in the return of the month in which the note is issued.
